h1: AI Product Photo Generator: Listings and Scenes
lead: This AI product photo generator puts your product in a new background, a white catalog shot, or a lifestyle scene. Check it against the item you ship, then post it.
summary: You skip a second shoot. One sharp photo becomes a new setting, a white catalog shot, or the product with a person. Match it to the item you ship, then post it.

sections.h2: A Fresh Setting for Your Product
paras: Your product can sit in new light without a second shoot. The bag in this photo sits beside a scarf on the entry table. Ask for late-afternoon light, a plain room, or an outdoor setup. If the shape changes, throw that file out.
Begin with one sharp photo. Name the surface and the light, then compare the result with the item you ship. Open the [photo tools](page:photo-hub) once the source photo is sharp.

sections.h2: How to Make a Product Photo in 3 Simple Steps
paras: Upload Your Product Photo. A phone picture on a pale surface is enough, like the bag standing upright in this frame. If you would rather not upload yet, write one sentence about a clean surface and soft light.
Describe Your Scene. Ask for the product alone on white when you need the first image on the product page. Ask for a hand lifting it only when you want a use shot. Say the look in plain words.

Download and Post. When the product looks right, download the square file. If an edge or a piece of hardware looks wrong, write a shorter note and run it again. That still can later be the first frame of a clip.

sections.h2: What One Product Photo Can Cover
paras: One photo can cover the product page and a paid post, without a second shoot. The bag in this picture, on a sunlit desk beside a folded sweater, can do both jobs. The item in the file still has to match the item you ship.

A new product page wants more than one picture. A seasonal post wants a new setting. A supplier photo may not match the rest of the store. When a buyer must see stitching or hardware, a close-up you photographed is still the safer file.

sections.h2: Where Should Each Product Photo Go?
paras: A marketplace hero and a social post can come from the same photo, once you pick the destination. A marketplace hero has stricter rules than a social post. The cafe scene in this photo is the social version.

A first image usually wants a clean white field and nothing extra in the frame. Later photos can show the product in a box, in use, or as a detail. On your own store, match the backdrop you already use so the row stays tidy. A square file fits a product page and a social crop, and you can also pick 9:16, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4.
sections.alt: A woman with short hair sits at a cafe table beside your tan handbag, a coffee cup, and sunglasses.

sections.h2: How Do I Check a Photo Before I Publish It?
paras: Put the image beside the real product in your hand. Compare color, shape, hardware, and how many pieces there are. The bag in this photo is the one you check.

Zoom in on the label, the hardware, and the edges. If something is wrong, run it again from a sharper photo or a clearer sentence instead of hiding it with a caption. Use your own label and your own logo. The picture should say only what is really on the product. The [Content Policy](/content) says what can be uploaded. Uploads and results stay in your account and are not shown publicly.
sections.alt: Hands check your tan handbag beside a blank phone before you post the photo.

sections.h2: A Product Photo You Can Publish
paras: One daylight photo, plus a plain sentence, gives you the next scene to post. Compare it with the real product before it goes on the product page.
White images and room scenes are separate jobs. A finished image can run in ads and on your store, and it does not carry a watermark.
